panels.title: Business Metrics — what the pipeline is producing
ClickHouse: Event count per window
panels.description: Sum of order_count (every event of any type, not just purchases) across all category/country rows in each 30s window, as it lands in ClickHouse. This is the 'watch it update' goal for the full-throughput stress test — revenue is no longer meaningful on its own since most event types don't carry an amount.

targets.rawSql: SELECT window_start AS time, sum(order_count) AS event_count FROM stream_processing_project.windowed_revenue GROUP BY window_start ORDER BY window_start

panels.title: ClickHouse: windowed_revenue insert rate
panels.description: Rows inserted per minute, by actual insert time (not window time) — shows sink write latency/throughput directly, complementing the Flink busy/backpressure panel.

targets.rawSql: SELECT toStartOfMinute(inserted_at) AS time, count() AS rows_inserted FROM stream_processing_project.windowed_revenue GROUP BY time ORDER BY time

panels.title: ClickHouse: End-to-end Latency over time (window_end -> inserted_at)
panels.description: Live time-series version of the avg/max latency report_pipeline_metrics() prints once at the end of a run — this shows the trend live, during the run, not just a post-hoc summary. Latency here is the time from a window closing (window_end) to that window's row becoming visible in ClickHouse: dominated by watermark_seconds (how long Flink waits past window_end before firing) plus real processing/sink overhead — NOT window_seconds, which only controls how long each window spans, not how long results take to appear after closing.

targets.rawSql: SELECT window_start AS time, avg(dateDiff('second', window_end, inserted_at)) AS avg_latency_s, max(dateDiff('second', window_end, inserted_at)) AS max_latency_s FROM stream_processing_project.windowed_revenue GROUP BY window_start ORDER BY window_start

panels.title: ClickHouse: raw_events insert rate (events/sec)
panels.description: count() per 5s bucket, by inserted_at — real end-to-end throughput for scenario 1's per-event passthrough job (raw_event_sink.py), directly comparable to Broker Bytes In/sec (÷ ~1099 bytes/event) and the windowed_revenue Events/sec panel above. Only populated during scenario 1 (or any run of raw_event_sink.py); the windowed_revenue panels above stay empty during scenario 1 since that job never writes to windowed_revenue.

targets.rawSql: SELECT toStartOfInterval(inserted_at, INTERVAL 5 SECOND) AS time, count() / 5.0 AS events_per_sec FROM stream_processing_project.raw_events GROUP BY time ORDER BY time

panels.title: ClickHouse: raw_events End-to-end Latency (event_time -> inserted_at)
panels.description: True single-event pipeline latency (Kafka + Flink + ClickHouse overhead only, no windowing wait) — the live version of what latency_breakdown.py reports once at the end of a run. Millisecond-precision (both event_time and inserted_at are DateTime64(3)), reported as fractional seconds since values are typically sub-few-second here. Compare against the windowed_revenue latency panel above to see how much of that latency is windowing wait vs real pipeline overhead.

targets.rawSql: SELECT toStartOfMinute(inserted_at) AS time, avg(dateDiff('millisecond', event_time, inserted_at)) / 1000.0 AS avg_latency_s, max(dateDiff('millisecond', event_time, inserted_at)) / 1000.0 AS max_latency_s FROM stream_processing_project.raw_events GROUP BY time ORDER BY time

panels.title: Broker Bytes In/sec (JMX — true broker measurement)
Flink Records In/Out per sec (windowed-revenue job)
panels.description: 'kafka ingest' uses the OPERATOR-scoped metric (operator_name="Source:_kafka_clickstream") — the Source operator alone — so it reflects ALL events Flink reads from Kafka, comparable 1:1 with Broker Bytes In/sec (÷ ~1099 bytes avg = events/sec). Since the job no longer filters to purchase-only (processes every event type, a deliberate full-throughput stress test — see CONTEXT.md), 'kafka ingest' and 'window+sink out' should now track each other closely, unlike before when the purchase filter made the two differ by ~15-20x. A growing gap between them would mean the window+sink stage (including the ClickHouse sink) can't keep up with full Kafka volume. Computed as rate() over raw cumulative counters, not Flink's own numRecordsInPerSecond/numRecordsOutPerSecond gauges, which stayed at 0 in testing despite real throughput.

panels.title: Flink Task Busy vs Backpressured Time (ms/sec)
panels.description: Backpressure here means the sink (ClickHouse insert) can't keep up with the window+sink task, or the source can't keep up with Kafka.

panels.title: Flink Network Buffer Pool Usage (%)
panels.description: outPoolUsage/inPoolUsage — the canonical Flink backpressure signal per its own docs, reacting earlier than busy/backpressured time since buffers fill up before a task visibly spends time backpressured. Sustained high outPoolUsage on a task means its downstream can't drain fast enough (e.g. the ClickHouse sink can't keep up with the window task's output).

panels.title: Flink Late Records Dropped (cumulative, window operator)
panels.description: Raw cumulative numLateRecordsDropped on the window operator — events whose window had already fired (watermark passed window_end) by the time they arrived, and were silently dropped (no allowedLateness/side-output configured). Deliberately NOT rate()-smoothed: a rate() over a 30s window turns a single drop (e.g. scenario 4's one truly-late test event) into ~0.033/sec, visually indistinguishable from 0 on a normal scale. This raw counter instead shows a clear step up that stays visible, making a single drop easy to confirm at a glance.

panels.title: Flink TaskManager JVM Heap Used vs Max
panels.description: Flink's own JVM health — we've monitored the Kafka broker's JVM (heap/GC/CPU) via JMX since early on, but never Flink's own taskmanager, which is just as capable of GC-thrashing or running low on heap under load.

panels.title: Flink TaskManager JVM GC Pause Rate (ms/sec)
panels.description: Same signal we already track for the Kafka broker's JVM (JVM GC Pause Rate) — mirrored here for Flink's own taskmanager. Spikes here would show up as processing stalls/latency in the pipeline, indistinguishable from a real bottleneck unless you know to check this.

panels.title: Flink Checkpoint Duration (ms) / Size (bytes)
panels.description: Checkpointing is on by default (see CONTEXT.md) — this was completely dark before. Duration is the direct 'how expensive is this interval' number for scenario 5's interval tradeoff; size shows how much state has accumulated.

panels.title: Flink Job Restarts
panels.description: numRestarts — should stay flat during normal operation and tick up exactly once per deliberate failure (e.g. scenario 5's `docker restart flink-taskmanager` kill-and-recover test). An unexpected increase here means the job failed and recovered without you noticing.

panels.title: ClickHouse: New Parts vs Merges per minute
panels.description: From system.part_log (historical, not a live snapshot). Each INSERT creates one new part (NewPart); background merges combine them (MergeParts). If new_parts consistently outpaces merges, unmerged parts accumulate — the leading indicator of the 'too many parts' problem, visible here before it ever surfaces as a throttled insert rate or a DB::Exception. A sustained gap explains the scenario 1 throughput/latency degradation investigated 2026-07-31 (uncapped producer + fixed sink_batch_rows=200 outpacing merge capacity).

targets.rawSql: SELECT toStartOfMinute(event_time) AS time, countIf(event_type = 'NewPart') AS new_parts, countIf(event_type = 'MergeParts') AS merges FROM system.part_log WHERE database = 'stream_processing_project' AND event_time > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR GROUP BY time ORDER BY time

panels.title: ClickHouse: Active Parts Count (live)
panels.description: Current active part count per table, from system.parts (a live snapshot, not historical — each dashboard refresh (5s) appends one new point, so the trend only builds up while this panel is being viewed). A steadily climbing count during a run, not settling back down between refreshes, means merges are falling behind inserts. ClickHouse's own defaults start delaying inserts around 300 parts per partition and throwing an exception around 3000 — this panel is the direct signal to watch before hitting either threshold.

targets.rawSql: SELECT now() AS time, table, count() AS active_parts FROM system.parts WHERE active AND database = 'stream_processing_project' GROUP BY table
